core.title: Used car condition-value joint evaluation method based on multiagent LLM decision tree collaboration
core.venue: International Conference on Machine Learning, Neural Networks and Computer Software
core.abstract: This research investigates a multi-agent big language model decision tree collaboration-based used automobile conditionvalue joint evaluation approach. All kinds of data, including vehicle age, mileage, maintenance records, inspection reports, accident history, market pricing, and vendor details, are arranged in this manner. A pricing agent calculates the market value, a risk agent modifies hidden-loss factors, an explanation agent produces reviewable evidence, and a condition agent retrieves vehicle-state evidence. The reasoning route is constrained by a decision tree, and rather of producing free-form text, the result value adheres to interpretable constraints. The suggested approach increased condition-grade consistency from 81.6% to 89.2%, lowered high-risk missing instances by 6.1%, and decreased mean absolute valuation error from 8.7% to 5.4% in a simulated used automobile transaction dataset. According to the aforementioned findings, decision-tree restrictions and cooperative agents can improve the valuation's interpretability and stability.

core.title: QMIX-based multiagent reinforcement learning with LLM-driven negotiation for urban facility location optimization
core.venue: International Conference on Machine Learning, Neural Networks and Computer Software
core.abstract: Urban renewal requires intelligent service facility reconfiguration to balance accessibility, cost and stakeholder preferences. Traditional optimization models lack adaptability to dynamic contexts and qualitative inputs. This paper proposes a novel framework integrating Large Language Models (LLMs) with multi-agent collaboration for the facility location problem, formulating it as a p-median model enhanced by LLM-derived dynamic demand weighting and multi-agent reinforcement learning. Experiments on a synthetic urban dataset show 94.2% coverage efficiency and 23.4% lower negotiation overhead, indicating LLM-enhanced multi-agent systems are promising for intelligent urban infrastructure planning.

core.title: Cohort Divergence Does Not Consistently Outperform Single-Rollout Judging for Early Warning of LLM Agent Failure
core.abstract: Early warning of failure would let costly episodes of large language model (LLM) agents be stopped early. Across five model families and five domains (3421 usable rollouts), we test a black-box signal: a rollout’s early divergence in judged goal adherence from sibling rollouts of the same task. Under our original judging protocol, cohort divergence predicted failure. A judge swap revealed the judge had received a task identifier instead of the task objective. Re-judged with the correct objective, the cohort signal fell to chance in retail and airline. A single-rollout judge score has the higher point estimate in eight of ten domain-horizon combinations; only contrasts favouring it survive Holm adjustment. Cohort features add 0.02 held-out AUROC, accounted for by the sibling mean and consistent with task-difficulty information; no per-domain gain survives adjustment. No pre-specified failure-onset profile is confirmed, and a perturbation experiment is inconclusive. Both monitors use privileged access to the full objective; restricted to information the agent had seen, most of their signal disappears. Under an enforced false-abort cap, no monitor has a usable operating point on the original score scale; a finer scale restores conservative ones for four of five models. Judge scores were not validated against human ratings. Judge instructions are a first-order threat to validity in agent-monitoring research.

core.title: RECAP: Regression Evaluation for Continual Adaptation of Prompts
core.abstract: Production agentic systems routinely face evolving constraints and must comply from the very next interaction. Scenarios like a tool-call notification changing a compliance threshold or a policy update adding disclosure requirements fit this criteria, having close to no room for errors in production. This proactive adaptation setting is common in deployment, but absent from current benchmarks, which assume either static constraint sets or reactive protocols with evaluation feedback. We introduce RECAP, a benchmark that measures continual-learning phenomena (forgetting, regression, forward transfer) at the constraint level under a strictly proactive adapt-then-test protocol: prompt optimization methods receive only the constraint specification and must generalize before seeing any test data. Evaluating six methods across five LLMs and three schedules with evolving constraints, we find that these methods show no significant improvement in performance, even after incurring a higher latency. These methods, designed for offline or reactive settings, are inadequate for the proactive paradigm. Our work emphasizes the growing need for designing proactive prompt adaptation methods, where the models must remain robust to evolving needs in deployment.

core.title: REAT: A Reflective Experience-Augmented Tutoring Framework for Multi-turn Mathematical Instruction
core.abstract: Current Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at solving complex mathematical problems, yet this proficiency does not inherently translate into effective tutoring. While advanced LLM tutors may leverage multi-agent frameworks or fine-tuning, most still lack a mechanism to systematically accumulate and reuse pedagogical experience over time, limiting their adaptability to diverse student needs during fluid, multi-turn interactions. To bridge this gap, we propose the Reflective Experience-Augmented Tutoring (REAT) framework, which couples experience distillation from historical dialogues with real-time adaptive retrieval. Driven by a multi-agent Observer-Critic-Mentor (OCM) distillation pipeline, REAT reviews past conversational trajectories and distills raw interactions into structured, problem-agnostic pedagogical experiences. During live tutoring, a state-aware retrieval module injects these curated experiences to provide adaptive scaffolding based on the student’s cognitive state. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework significantly outperforms both prompt-only and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baselines, particularly in improving complex, low-scoring teaching scenarios. Crucially, the distilled experiences exhibit robust generalization across diverse model architectures and mathematical datasets.

core.title: Read the Paper, Write the Code: Agentic Reproduction of Social-Science Results
core.abstract: Recent work uses LLM agents to reproduce empirical social science results with access to both the data and code. We broaden this scope by asking: Can they reproduce results given only a paper’s methods description and original data? We develop an agentic reproduction system that extracts structured methods descriptions from papers, runs reimplementations under strict information isolation—agents never see the original code, results, or paper—and enables deterministic, cell-level comparison of reproduced outputs to the original results. An LLM-based attribution step traces discrepancies through the system chain to identify root causes. Evaluating four agent scaffolds and four LLMs on 48 papers with human-verified reproducibility, we find that agents can largely recover published results, but performance varies substantially between models, scaffolds, and papers. Root cause analysis suggests that failures stem both from agent errors and from underspecification in the papers themselves.

papers.title: Read the Paper, Write the Code: Agentic Reproduction of Social-Science Results
papers.abstract: Recent work uses LLM agents to reproduce empirical social science results with access to both the data and code. We broaden this scope by asking: Can they reproduce results given only a paper’s methods description and original data? We develop an agentic reproduction system that extracts structured methods descriptions from papers, runs reimplementations under strict information isolation—agents never see the original code, results, or paper—and enables deterministic, cell-level comparison of reproduced outputs to the original results. An LLM-based attribution step traces discrepancies through the system chain to identify root causes. Evaluating four agent scaffolds and four LLMs on 48 papers with human-verified reproducibility, we find that agents can largely recover published results, but performance varies substantially between models, scaffolds, and papers. Root cause analysis suggests that failures stem both from agent errors and from underspecification in the papers themselves.
